questions.question: What is a key architectural feature of the Sun Temple at Modhera?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Stepped tank**__.
 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 __ 
• **The Sun Temple at Modhera**, located in Gujarat, India, is a remarkable example of ancient Indian temple architecture built during the reign of the Chalukya dynasty under King Bhima I in **1026-27 CE**. 
• A defining feature of this temple is its massive and intricately designed **stepped tank (Surya Kund)**, which served as a sacred water reservoir for devotees to perform ablutions before entering the temple. 
• The stepped tank is geometrically designed with **terraces, symmetrical steps, and numerous small shrines** carved into the steps, showcasing exceptional craftsmanship and symmetry. 
• The tank is divided into multiple **rectangular and square tiers**, with steps descending in a pyramid-like fashion, creating a visually stunning layout that enhances the temple's aesthetic appeal. 
• The **stepped tank** not only had religious significance but also served as a water conservation system, demonstrating the advanced engineering and ecological awareness of the time. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 __ 
• **Other Architectural Features of the Sun Temple:** 
• The temple is designed in the **Māru-Gurjara architectural style**, characterized by intricate carvings, ornate pillars, and detailed sculptures. 
• The main sanctum (Garbhagriha) was constructed in such a way that the first rays of the sun would illuminate the deity, symbolizing the temple's dedication to the Sun God. 
• The Sabha Mandapa (assembly hall) is a **pillared hall** with exquisitely carved pillars and arches, showcasing stories from Hindu mythology. 
• The temple is divided into three main components: **Garbhagriha** (sanctum), **Gudha Mandapa** (main hall), and **Kunda** (stepped tank). 
• **Significance of Stepped Tanks in Indian Architecture:** 
• Stepped tanks, also known as **Kunds** or **Pushkarnis**, were a common feature of ancient Indian temples and served both religious and utilitarian purposes. 
• They were used for **ritual purification**, community gatherings, and water conservation. 
• These tanks often contained **small shrines** dedicated to deities, adding to their religious significance. 
• Famous examples of stepped tanks include the **Rani ki Vav** in Patan and the **Chand Baori** in Rajasthan. 
• **Details about Incorrect Options:** 
• **Gopuram:** This is a monumental entrance tower commonly found in South Indian temples, especially in Tamil Nadu. It is not a feature of the Sun Temple at Modhera. 
• **Garuda Pillar:** A tall pillar often dedicated to Garuda, the mount of Lord Vishnu, is typically found in Vaishnavite temples but is not a key feature of this temple. 
• **Vimana:** This refers to the tower above the sanctum in South Indian temple architecture. The Sun Temple at Modhera does not have a Vimana as it is built in the Māru-Gurjara style. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
• The Sun Temple at Modhera is a **UNESCO World Heritage Site** and a popular tourist attraction. 
• The temple is aligned in such a way that during equinoxes, the first rays of the sun illuminate the idol in the sanctum. 
• The site is an excellent example of **water management systems** in ancient India, combining aesthetics and functionality. 
• The Modhera Dance Festival is held annually near the temple, celebrating the region's rich cultural heritage.

questions.question: The traditional folk festival 'Phuldei', marked by floral offerings and cultural rituals, is primarily observed in which Indian state?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Uttarakhand**__.
 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 __ 
• **Phuldei** is a traditional **folk festival** celebrated in the Indian state of **Uttarakhand**, primarily observed during the month of **March** to mark the arrival of spring. 
• It is a festival where young children visit houses in their villages and offer **flowers**, grains, and rice to the house's threshold, wishing prosperity and happiness for the inhabitants. 
• The festival is deeply rooted in the **cultural and religious traditions** of Uttarakhand and reflects the close bond between the people and nature. 
• Phuldei is celebrated with various **rituals and songs**. Children sing folk songs while offering floral tributes, and families prepare traditional dishes such as **‘Puri’ and ‘Singal’**. 
• This festival symbolizes **community harmony, gratitude, and the celebration of nature**, which are integral to the culture of Uttarakhand. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 
• **Uttarakhand:** 
• Uttarakhand, also known as the **"Devbhoomi" (Land of Gods)**, is a northern state in India, famous for its **natural beauty, religious heritage, and vibrant folk traditions**. 
• The state is rich in **flora and fauna**, and its traditions often revolve around the celebration of nature. 
• Other notable festivals celebrated in Uttarakhand include **Harela, Bikhauti, and Khatarua**. 
• Uttarakhand is divided into two regions: **Kumaon** and **Garhwal**, each having its own unique cultural practices and festivals. 
• The state offers picturesque landscapes, such as the **Himalayas, rivers (like Ganga and Yamuna), and forests**, making it a significant tourist destination. 
• **Other Indian States:** 
• **Himachal Pradesh:** Known for its snow-clad mountains and vibrant festivals like **Losar, Kullu Dussehra, and Minjar**. 
• **Jammu and Kashmir:** Famous for its festivals such as **Navroz, Eid, and Tulip Festival**, and its cultural diversity. 
• **Assam:** Celebrates festivals like **Bihu, Ambubachi Mela**, and **Durga Puja**, reflecting its rich tradition and agricultural significance. 
• **Punjab:** Known for its energetic festivals like **Lohri, Baisakhi**, and **Gurpurab**, showcasing the vibrancy of Punjabi culture. 
• **Important Points:** 
• Festivals like Phuldei highlight the **importance of preserving cultural heritage** and **environmental conservation**. 
• They provide a unique opportunity for communities to come together and celebrate their traditions, fostering **social unity**. 
• Traditional festivals often incorporate **seasonal changes**, agricultural practices, and gratitude towards nature, making them both culturally and ecologically significant.

questions.question: Which of the following sculptures does not originate from the Mathura region's Kushana-period artistic production?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Bala Buddha of Sultanganj**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__

• The **Bala Buddha of Sultanganj** is a sculpture that does not originate from the **Mathura region's Kushana-period artistic production**.

• It is a famous bronze sculpture from the **Gupta period** (5th–6th century CE) and was discovered in **Sultanganj, Bihar**, not Mathura.

• The other sculptures mentioned in the options, such as the **Katra Keshav Dev fragment**, **Govind Nagar Yaksha**, and the **Standing Buddha from Govindnagar**, are directly linked to the **Mathura school of art** during the Kushana period.

• The Mathura school of art during the Kushana period (1st–3rd century CE) was known for its production of red sandstone sculptures and its unique style of depicting Buddha and other deities.

• The **Bala Buddha of Sultanganj**, being a Gupta-period artifact, showcases a different artistic style and geographical origin, which differentiates it from the Mathura Kushana-period sculptures.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__

• **Mathura School of Art:**

• It flourished during the **Kushana period (1st–3rd century CE)** and was centered in Mathura, Uttar Pradesh.

• Known for its production of **sculptures in red sandstone**, it depicted Buddhist, Jain, and Hindu deities.

• Key features include the **depiction of Buddha** with a distinctive smile, **spiritual calmness**, and **ornamentation**.

• Examples include the **Standing Buddha from Govindnagar** and the **Govind Nagar Yaksha**.

• **Bala Buddha of Sultanganj:**

• A famous bronze statue from the **Gupta period (5th–6th century CE)**, discovered in Sultanganj, Bihar.

• It is about **2.3 meters tall** and is one of the largest surviving bronze sculptures from ancient India.

• The statue is currently housed in the **Birmingham Museum and Art Gallery** in the United Kingdom.

• It represents the Gupta style of art, which is known for its **refined and graceful depictions of religious figures**.

• **Kushana Art Characteristics:**

• The Kushana period saw the emergence of two major schools of art: the **Mathura school** and the **Gandhara school**.

• The Mathura school focused on **native Indian art traditions**, while the Gandhara school incorporated **Greco-Roman influences**.

• Sculptures from this period are known for their **iconographic innovations** and the introduction of the anthropomorphic form of Buddha.

• **Comparison of Styles:**

• The **Mathura school** is characterized by **red sandstone sculptures** with an emphasis on spirituality and indigenous elements.

• The **Gupta period art**, including the Bala Buddha of Sultanganj, is known for its **refinement, grace, and emphasis on idealized human forms**.

• The Gupta art style marked the culmination of artistic development in ancient India, often referred to as the **Golden Age of Indian Art**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• **Katra Keshav Dev Fragment:** Belongs to the Mathura school of art and represents the indigenous style of the Kushana period.

• **Govind Nagar Yaksha:** A prominent example of Mathura art that reflects early Kushana-period artistry.

• **Standing Buddha from Govindnagar:** A red sandstone sculpture that embodies the Mathura style's anthropomorphic depiction of Buddha.

• **Bala Buddha of Sultanganj:** A Gupta-period bronze sculpture discovered in Bihar, showcasing advanced metallurgical and artistic techniques.

 __ 
• **Ibn Battuta**, a Moroccan traveller, visited India during the reign of **Mohammad bin Tughlaq** in the 14th century. 
• He documented his experiences in his travelogue called **"Rihla" (The Journey)**, which provides detailed insights into the social, political, and cultural aspects of regions he visited. 
• In his accounts, Ibn Battuta described how **Indian chieftains used bamboo groves** and rugged terrains for fortifications as part of their defence strategies.

 __ 
• **Article 360** of the Indian Constitution provides the framework for declaring a **Financial Emergency** when the financial stability or credit of India or any part of its territory is threatened. 
• **No Financial Emergency** has ever been declared in India since the adoption of the Constitution in 1950. *(Statement 1 is correct)* 
• Under a Financial Emergency, the **President of India** can direct the reduction of salaries and allowances of all or any class of persons serving the Union or a State, including the **judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts**. *(Statement 1 is correct)*

• All money bills and financial bills passed by the State Legislature can be reserved for the President's consideration. 
• The President can direct the State to observe financial propriety measures. 
• **Proclamation of Financial Emergency:** 
• A Financial Emergency can be proclaimed under Article 360 by the President if satisfied that the financial stability or credit of India or its territory is threatened. 
• The proclamation must be approved by both Houses of Parliament within two months.

• India has dealt with economic crises in the past, such as in **1991**, through policy measures rather than invoking constitutional emergencies.

questions.question: What is the audible frequency range for the human ear?

__

• The **audible frequency range for the human ear** typically spans from **20 Hz to 20,000 Hz**. This range is considered the standard for human hearing across different age groups and conditions.

• Frequencies below **20 Hz** are referred to as **infrasound**, and frequencies above **20,000 Hz** are called **ultrasound**. These are outside the range of human hearing.

• The sensitivity of human hearing varies with frequency. Humans are most sensitive to sounds in the range of approximately **2 kHz to 5 kHz**, which corresponds to everyday sounds like speech.

• As humans age, the ability to hear higher frequencies diminishes. For instance, older individuals may lose sensitivity to sounds above **15,000 Hz**.

• The audible range is crucial for various applications such as **speech communication, music, and acoustic engineering**, ensuring devices like headphones and speakers cater to this range.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• **Characteristics of Human Hearing:** 

• Humans can perceive both **pitch (frequency)** and **intensity (loudness)** of sound waves within the audible range.

• The **threshold of hearing** (minimum audible sound) is around **0 dB**, while the threshold of pain is approximately **120-130 dB**.

• Hearing ability is influenced by factors such as **age, environment, and health conditions**.

• **Infrasound:** 

• Frequencies below **20 Hz** are known as infrasound. These are produced by natural phenomena like **earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, and ocean waves**.

• Though humans cannot hear infrasound, it can be felt as vibrations and has applications in **seismic monitoring**.

• **Ultrasound:** 

• Frequencies above **20,000 Hz** are termed ultrasound. It is widely used in **medical imaging, industrial applications, and cleaning**.

• Animals such as **bats and dolphins** can hear ultrasound and utilize it for navigation and communication.

• **Applications of Audible Range Knowledge:** 

• Design of audio equipment like **microphones, speakers, and headphones** is based on the human audible range.

• Technological advancements in fields like **telecommunications, music production, and hearing aids** rely on understanding the auditory spectrum.

• **Important Facts:** 

• The **human auditory system** includes the outer ear, middle ear, and inner ear, working together to process sound waves.

• The study of human hearing is essential in disciplines such as **audiology, acoustics, and psychoacoustics**.

• Hearing tests, such as **pure tone audiometry**, are used to determine the audible frequency range of individuals.

• **Revenue Expenditure** refers to the expenses incurred by the government for its day-to-day functioning, such as salaries, subsidies, interest payments, and grants.

• **Grants for asset creation**, although they might lead to the creation of assets, are considered revenue expenditure because these assets are not owned by the central government but by other entities like state governments, local bodies, or private organizations.

• The grants are **used to support projects or schemes** implemented by other entities, and the central government does not directly derive ownership or control over the created assets.

• Such expenditures are categorized under revenue expenditure as they do not contribute to the **direct creation of tangible central assets** but rather facilitate broader developmental goals through financial assistance.

• This classification aligns with **accounting principles** and government budgetary norms, where the ownership and control of the resultant asset determine whether an expenditure is capital or revenue.

• Expenditure is **recurring in nature** and does not result in the creation of physical assets.

• Examples: Salaries of government employees, maintenance of infrastructure, and grants to state governments or NGOs.

• **Capital Expenditure:** 

• Capital expenditure involves **investment in assets** or projects that provide benefits over a long period.

• Examples include building infrastructure like roads, bridges, and power plants.

• It is considered an investment in the economic capacity of the nation and is reflected in the government’s asset accounts.

• **Grants for Asset Creation:** 

• Such grants are provided by the central government to **state governments, local bodies, or private organizations** to assist in the creation of specific assets or projects.

• The ownership of these assets does not remain with the central government, and thus the grants are recorded as **revenue expenditure**.

• Examples: Grants for rural infrastructure, urban development projects, or welfare schemes.

• **Budgetary Classification:** 

• Government budgets classify expenditures into **revenue** and **capital** to ensure transparency and proper monitoring of public finances.

• Revenue expenditure affects the government’s **revenue deficit**, while capital expenditure impacts the **fiscal deficit**.

• **Key Differences:** 

• **Revenue expenditure:** Short-term benefits, recurring, no asset creation.

• **Capital expenditure:** Long-term benefits, non-recurring, leads to asset creation.

• **Accounting Standards:** Government accounting guidelines distinguish between revenue and capital expenditure based on asset ownership and the duration of benefits.

• **Examples of Revenue Expenditure:** Grants for rural employment schemes (e.g., MGNREGA), subsidies for fertilizers, and interest payments on loans.

• **Impact on Budget:** High revenue expenditure can lead to a higher **revenue deficit**, indicating a need for better fiscal management.

• **Policy Implications:** Classifying grants for asset creation as revenue expenditure emphasizes the importance of ownership in determining the nature of government spending.

Read the below statements marked as Assertion (A) and Reason (R). Mark the correct option:

Assertion (A): CRR (Cash Reserve Ratio) and SLR requirements increase the lending capacity of banks.

Reason (R): These requirements reduce the amount of money banks can lend to the public.

options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**4) A is false, but R is true.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__

• **Assertion (A): CRR (Cash Reserve Ratio) and SLR requirements increase the lending capacity of banks.** - This statement is **false**. CRR and SLR requirements, instead of increasing the lending capacity, reduce the amount of money that banks can lend to the public. Banks are mandated to keep a certain percentage of their deposits as reserves, thereby limiting the funds available for lending.

• **Reason (R): These requirements reduce the amount of money banks can lend to the public.** - This statement is **true**. Both CRR and SLR are regulatory mechanisms aimed at ensuring liquidity and financial stability. By mandating banks to maintain reserves, they restrict the banks' ability to lend excessively, thus reducing the lending capacity.

• **CRR (Cash Reserve Ratio):** - It is the percentage of total deposits that banks are required to keep with the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) as reserves. This is done to ensure liquidity in the banking system and control inflation.

• **SLR (Statutory Liquidity Ratio):** - It is the percentage of net demand and time liabilities (NDTL) that banks must maintain in the form of liquid assets like cash, gold, or government-approved securities. SLR ensures financial stability and liquidity.

• **Correct Explanation:** - The Reason (R) correctly explains the impact of CRR and SLR requirements on banks' lending capacity, as these requirements directly reduce the funds available for lending by the banks.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__

• **CRR (Cash Reserve Ratio):** 

• CRR is set by the **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)** and currently ranges between 3% to 5%, depending on the economic situation.

• Higher CRR helps control inflation by reducing liquidity, while lower CRR boosts economic growth by increasing liquidity.

• Banks do not earn any interest on the funds kept as CRR with the RBI.

• **SLR (Statutory Liquidity Ratio):** 

• SLR is also regulated by the RBI and is generally maintained between 18% to 23% of NDTL.

• Unlike CRR, banks earn returns on the assets maintained under SLR, such as government securities.

• SLR serves as a tool for regulating inflation and ensuring the financial stability of banks.

• **Key Objectives of CRR and SLR:** 

• Control liquidity in the economy.

• Ensure financial stability and prevent excessive lending by banks.

• Help the government in borrowing funds by mandating banks to invest in government securities.

• **Impact on the Economy:** 

• Both CRR and SLR play a crucial role in monetary policy implementation.

• Higher reserves reduce inflationary pressures but may slow down economic growth.

• Lower reserves increase liquidity and boost lending but may lead to inflation.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• **Difference Between CRR and SLR:** 

• **CRR:** Funds are kept with the RBI; banks earn no interest.

• **SLR:** Funds are invested in liquid assets like government securities; banks earn returns.

• **Impact on Lending:** 

• Higher CRR and SLR reduce banks' ability to lend, curbing liquidity in the economy.

• Lower CRR and SLR increase lending capacity, promoting economic growth.

• **Examples of Application:** 

• During inflationary periods, CRR and SLR are increased to reduce liquidity.

• During economic slowdown, CRR and SLR are reduced to enhance liquidity and boost lending.

• **Sustainable Development Goals Index:**
 
 
• The **SDG Index** ranks countries annually based on their progress toward achieving the 17 SDGs.
 
• It uses metrics such as **healthcare access, education quality, renewable energy use, and environmental conservation** to evaluate performance.
 
• This index is a central feature of the **UN Sustainable Development Report**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Key Features of the SDGs:**

 
 
• The SDGs apply to all countries, emphasizing **universal goals** rather than being limited to developing nations.
 
• They integrate **social, economic, and environmental dimensions** of sustainable development.
 
• Each goal has specific **indicators and targets** to measure progress.
 
 
 
• **Global Partnerships:**
 
 
• The SDGs highlight the importance of **collaborative efforts** across governments, NGOs, private sector, and academia.
 
• Goal 17 specifically emphasizes **Partnerships for the Goals** to mobilize resources for achieving the targets.
 
 
 
• **Challenges in Implementation:**
 
 
• Challenges include **data availability, financing gaps, political will, and global inequalities**.
 
• The **UN Sustainable Development Report** provides insights and recommendations to address these challenges.

questions.question: The rolling plan concept was introduced during which Prime Minister's tenure?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Morarji Desai**__.
 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 __ 
• The concept of a **Rolling Plan** was introduced during the tenure of **Morarji Desai**, who served as the Prime Minister of India from **1977 to 1979**. 
• A **Rolling Plan** implies that the plan would be dynamic and could be revised annually based on the country's economic performance and changing needs. 
• This approach was introduced as an alternative to the traditional **Five-Year Plans**, emphasizing flexibility in planning. 
• During Morarji Desai's tenure, the **Janata Party** government discarded the Fifth Five-Year Plan (1974–79) introduced by the previous government under Indira Gandhi. 
• The Rolling Plan was implemented for the years **1978–1980**, but it was discontinued after Indira Gandhi returned to power in **1980** and resumed the Five-Year Planning model. 
• The Rolling Plan was considered innovative as it focused on short-term adjustments rather than rigid long-term strategies, ensuring better responsiveness to economic fluctuations. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 __ 
• **Five-Year Plans in India:** 
• The concept of Five-Year Plans was introduced by the **Planning Commission of India** in **1951**, inspired by the Soviet model. 
• India's first Five-Year Plan (1951–56) focused on agriculture, irrigation, and community development. 
• Subsequent Five-Year Plans addressed various sectors, including industry, infrastructure, education, and health. 
• The Planning Commission was replaced by **NITI Aayog** in **2015** under the Narendra Modi government, ending the era of Five-Year Plans. 
• **Morarji Desai:** 
• Morarji Desai was India’s **fourth Prime Minister** and the first non-Congress leader to hold the position. 
• He served as Prime Minister from **March 1977 to July 1979** during the Janata Party government. 
• His tenure emphasized transparency, anti-corruption, and economic reforms. 
• He was awarded the **Bharat Ratna** in **1991** for his service to the nation. 
• **Concept of Rolling Plan:** 
• A Rolling Plan is a continuous plan that is updated annually or periodically to reflect changes in economic conditions and priorities. 
• It provides flexibility and adaptability, allowing policymakers to revise objectives and allocations in response to current developments. 
• This approach contrasts with fixed long-term plans, which may become outdated if circumstances change. 
• **Indira Gandhi’s Return to Five-Year Plans:** 
• When Indira Gandhi returned to power in **1980**, she reinstated the Five-Year Plan model, starting with the Sixth Five-Year Plan (1980–85). 
• Her approach focused on long-term planning to achieve sustained economic growth and development. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
• **Advantages of Rolling Plans:** 
• Provides flexibility to adjust to unforeseen economic changes. 
• Allows for more accurate forecasting and resource allocation. 
• Focuses on short-term goals while maintaining long-term objectives. 
• **Disadvantages of Rolling Plans:** 
• Frequent revisions can lead to administrative complications. 
• Lack of long-term vision may hinder sustained development. 
• Uncertainty in planning could impact investor confidence. 
• The Rolling Plan concept was eventually abandoned due to its challenges and inefficiencies compared to structured Five-Year Plans.

 __ 
• The **Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956** emphasized the concept of "commanding heights" of the economy, wherein core industries and key sectors were to be under the control of the state to ensure economic growth and equitable distribution of resources. 
• This policy classified industries into three categories: **Schedule A** (exclusively under state control), **Schedule B** (mixed state and private sector control), and **Schedule C** (open to private investment). 
• The resolution aimed to implement a **socialistic pattern of society**, focusing on reducing income inequalities and ensuring social justice by promoting state ownership in key sectors like steel, coal, and heavy machinery. 
• The **public sector** was envisioned to play a pivotal role in industrial development, while the private sector was expected to complement the efforts of the state in less critical sectors. 
• This policy laid the foundation for **planned economic development** in India, with the state playing a significant role in areas crucial for national security, infrastructure, and technological advancement. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 __ 
• **Key Features of the Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956:** 
• The resolution introduced the concept of **planned industrial development** under the purview of the state to achieve economic self-reliance. 
• It declared **17 industries** (such as iron and steel, atomic energy, heavy machinery, and defense production) exclusively reserved for the public sector under **Schedule A**. 
• **12 industries** were included in **Schedule B**, where both the state and private sectors could operate, with the state taking the lead in establishing new units. 
• All remaining industries were included in **Schedule C**, which were left open for private investment and initiatives. 
• Emphasis was placed on **small-scale industries** (SSI) to promote regional development and employment generation in rural areas. 
• **Objectives of the Policy:** 
• To accelerate the pace of industrialization and achieve **economic self-reliance**. 
• To reduce regional imbalances by ensuring equitable distribution of industries across the country. 
• To create employment opportunities and improve the standard of living for the masses. 
• To promote the **socialistic pattern of society** by reducing income inequalities and ensuring public ownership of key industries. 
• **Impact of the Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956:** 
• It laid the foundation for the **public sector-led industrial development** in India. 
• Key industries like steel, coal, and heavy engineering were established under state control, leading to the development of core infrastructure and capabilities. 
• The policy also promoted the **growth of small-scale industries**, which played a critical role in rural development and employment generation. 
• However, over time, the **dominance of the public sector** led to inefficiencies and stagnation, necessitating economic reforms in the 1990s.

• **Option 2: Import-led growth strategy** - The policy emphasized self-reliance and indigenous development, not an import-led strategy. 
• **Option 4: Promoting consumer goods industry** - While important, this was not the primary focus; heavy industries and infrastructure were prioritized.

__

• The primary short-term objective of the **1991 economic reforms** in India was to **control inflation** and address the crisis in the **balance of payments (BoP).** During this period, India was facing a severe economic crisis, with foreign exchange reserves falling to alarmingly low levels.

• By the early 1990s, **India's fiscal deficit** had ballooned to unsustainable levels, and the country was on the verge of defaulting on its external payments. The balance of payments crisis necessitated immediate corrective measures.

• The stabilization measures aimed to introduce **macroeconomic stability** by reducing fiscal deficits, controlling runaway inflation, and encouraging foreign investments to stabilize the economy.

• A key step in addressing the BoP crisis was to secure a loan from the **International Monetary Fund (IMF)** by pledging gold reserves and implementing structural adjustment reforms, including liberalization and deregulation of the economy.

• These stabilization measures were part of a broader set of **economic reforms**, including the liberalization of trade and industries, aimed at transitioning India toward a more open and market-driven economy.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__

• **Economic Background in 1991:**

• India faced a **severe fiscal and BoP crisis** in 1991, with foreign exchange reserves sufficient for less than three weeks of imports.

• The fiscal deficit was approximately **8.4% of GDP**, while inflation peaked at **17%** in August 1991.

• The Gulf War in 1990-91 further worsened the situation by increasing oil prices, leading to a sharp rise in import costs.

• **Key Components of Stabilization Measures:**

• **Devaluation of the Rupee (July 1991):** The Indian Rupee was devalued to encourage exports and reduce the trade deficit.

• **Reduction in fiscal deficit:** Government spending was curtailed, subsidies were reduced, and tax reforms were introduced to increase revenue.

• **Monetary tightening:** The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) adopted policies to control inflation by increasing interest rates and reducing money supply.

• **Trade liberalization:** Import restrictions were eased, and tariffs were lowered to promote competitiveness and attract foreign investments.

• **International Monetary Fund (IMF) Role:**

• India sought assistance from the **IMF**, which provided a loan of **$2.2 billion** under its structural adjustment program.

• The loan was conditional upon the implementation of **economic reforms**, including liberalization, privatization, and globalization (LPG).

• **Long-term Implications of the 1991 Reforms:**

• The reforms laid the foundation for India's transition to a **market-oriented economy.**

• India's GDP growth rate improved significantly, and foreign exchange reserves increased over time.

• The liberalization of industries and foreign trade paved the way for **foreign direct investment (FDI)** and technological advancements.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• **Other Objectives of the 1991 Reforms:**

• **Privatization:** Reducing the role of public sector enterprises and encouraging private sector participation in the economy.

• **Liberalization:** Removing barriers to trade, such as reducing import tariffs and allowing foreign investments in various sectors.

• **Globalization:** Integrating the Indian economy with the global economy by promoting exports and foreign trade.

• **Key Agencies and Policies Introduced:**

• The establishment of the **SEBI (Securities and Exchange Board of India)** to regulate the stock market and promote transparency.

• Introduction of the **New Industrial Policy of 1991**, which abolished the License Raj and reduced the number of industries reserved for the public sector.

• Reforms in the banking and financial sector to improve efficiency and encourage competition.

questions.question: The ratio of areas of two regular polygons with same number of sides is 4:9. What is the ratio of their side lengths?

questions.question: A line from the center of a circle bisects a chord. What is the angle between this line and the chord?
questions.solution:
[IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/ca81259519cadfb2d5350673c220e419e60378e9770ad26512fc8e826a8d93f1.png] __Shortcut Trick__

According to the standard circle theorem, a line drawn through the center of a circle to bisect a chord is always perpendicular to that chord.

Therefore, the angle formed between the bisecting line and the chord is exactly a right angle.

**∴ The correct answer is 90°.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/c76c13ba2d2ab46b47f8a931ae621dac081a0cb266b142dc23f58659fac4a466.png] **__Alternate Method__**

 
 
•

•

**Given:**

A circle with center O and chord AB.

A line OM drawn from the center bisects the chord AB, meaning AM = MB.

**Concept Used:**

Congruency of triangles using the SSS (Side-Side-Side) criterion.

**Calculations:**

⇒ In ΔOMA and ΔOMB:

⇒ OA = OB (Radii of the same circle)

⇒ AM = MB (Given that OM bisects the chord)

⇒ OM = OM (Common side)

⇒ By SSS congruence criterion, ΔOMA ≅ ΔOMB.

⇒ Therefore, their corresponding angles are equal: ∠OMA = ∠OMB.

⇒ Since AMB is a straight line, the sum of angles on the line is 180°.

⇒ ∠OMA + ∠OMB = 180°

⇒ 2 × ∠OMA = 180°

⇒ ∠OMA = 90°

**∴ The correct answer is 90°.**

Perpendicular from Center Theorem

The converse is also universally true: A perpendicular dropped from the center of a circle to a chord will always bisect the chord into two equal halves.

Equal Chords and Distance

Equal chords of a circle are always equidistant from the center. Conversely, chords that are equidistant from the center are equal in length.

Angle at the Center

The angle subtended by an arc at the center of a circle is double the angle subtended by it at any remaining part of the circle's circumference.

questions.question: A chord divides a circle into two arcs. The angle subtended by the major arc at the circumference is 110°. What is the central angle subtended by the major arc?

By the central angle theorem, the angle subtended by an arc at the center is exactly double the angle subtended by it at any point on the remaining part of the circle.

The major arc subtends an angle of 110° at the circumference (minor arc).

Central angle = 2 × Angle at circumference

Central angle = 2 × 110° = 220°

**∴ The correct answer is 220°.**
